scene: A repair shop needs a page that helps a visitor decide whether to contact it.

comparisons.title: A greeting or a useful message?
comparisons.notice: Read the page as someone looking for a repair. Which heading gives you useful information?
comparisons.takeaway: The browser displays the words you supply. A useful result starts with the visitor's need, even when AI writes the page.

comparisons.title: A different shop
comparisons.notice: Only the heading changes. The page still opens and its Contact action still works.
comparisons.takeaway: A change in the business can require different content without requiring a new database or a live AI call.

scene: The shop owner dislikes the page, but “make it impressive” leaves the builder guessing.

comparisons.title: Turn a feeling into a check

change.direction: Put opening hours below Services. Check that the hours are visible on a phone.

comparisons.notice: Look for a named part, an action and an observation someone can check.
comparisons.takeaway: Concrete direction gives a builder something to act on. This tiny word checker illustrates that pattern; it does not evaluate arbitrary instructions.

comparisons.title: Keep the change small

before.direction: Put opening hours below Services. Check that the hours are visible on a phone.

comparisons.notice: Keep the words identical. Change how much of the site the builder may alter.
comparisons.takeaway: A bounded change leaves unrelated decisions outside the task. Actual AI output still needs to be inspected.

scene: The shop wants a bigger heading. That is a different request from changing its words or its button's action.

comparisons.title: Appearance changes, words stay
comparisons.notice: Watch the heading grow. Read its words again; they have not changed.
comparisons.takeaway: Presentation and content have different jobs. Changing the CSS size need not change the HTML content.

comparisons.title: A button can look ready and do nothing
comparisons.notice: Try Contact in both cases. Compare its appearance with what actually happens.
comparisons.takeaway: A visible button does not prove that an action rule is present. Behaviour needs its own check.

scene: A visitor wants an estimate. The shop must decide which quantities are allowed before calculating a total.

comparisons.title: Blank is different from zero
comparisons.notice: Compare a zero total with a withheld total. Those results mean different things.
comparisons.takeaway: Zero is an allowed quantity in this rule. Blank means the visitor has not supplied an allowed quantity, so the model withholds the total.

comparisons.title: One more item
comparisons.notice: Count the item chips. One additional item adds one more unit price to the receipt.
comparisons.takeaway: The same multiplication rule works for each allowed whole quantity: quantity times price per item.

scene: The shop adds services. The page should create a card for each record using one display rule.

comparisons.title: Grow the collection
comparisons.notice: Count the records and cards. The display rule stays the same as the collection grows.
comparisons.takeaway: A loop applies the same rule to each record. More records do not require a separately written card for each one.

comparisons.title: Different cards, repeated identity
comparisons.notice: Inspect the cards marked Repeated ID. Their display labels cannot repair their repeated identifier.
comparisons.takeaway: Names and labels describe records. Stable, distinct identifiers let the system tell those records apart.

scene: The owner says customers miss visits. Before building a reminder, you need to know what supports that claim.

comparisons.title: An example or an observation?
comparisons.notice: The numbers stay identical. Inspect how the source changes what can be said about them.
comparisons.takeaway: An invented example shows a possibility. Checked fictional records describe this model sample, but still do not identify the cause of missed visits.

comparisons.title: Can the counts fit?
comparisons.notice: Try fitting two missed visits inside a sample containing only one visit.
comparisons.takeaway: Conflicting counts need investigation before calculating or interpreting a rate. A precise-looking percentage cannot repair inconsistent inputs.

scene: Two missed visits sound small, but the meaning depends on how many eligible visits there were.

comparisons.title: Keep the count; change the whole
comparisons.notice: The missed count stays at two. Watch the fraction and percentage change.
comparisons.takeaway: Two out of ten is 20%; two out of one hundred is 2%. The denominator changes the meaning of the same count.

comparisons.title: Unknown is not zero percent
comparisons.notice: Remove the eligible total. Look for Unknown rather than a reassuring zero.
comparisons.takeaway: A rate needs a usable denominator. Missing information should remain visible instead of silently becoming a favourable result.

scene: A customer is trying to request a visit. The form must help them recover when input or connectivity is missing.

comparisons.title: Give the form its required input
comparisons.notice: Follow the draft, connection and result steps before and after an identifier is present.
comparisons.takeaway: Required input is checked before the request proceeds in this model. A real confirmation still needs a real service response.

comparisons.title: Keep the draft when the connection fails
comparisons.notice: Read the draft after the connection fails. It should still contain V-42.
comparisons.takeaway: Keeping useful input and explaining the failure helps a person recover. A lost connection must not turn into an invented confirmation.

scene: The shop is choosing between a package and a custom build. Compare the same period and required capabilities.

comparisons.title: A repeating fee accumulates
comparisons.notice: Compare the growing package line with the fixed stated build cost.
comparisons.takeaway: The package's stated total reaches 600 units after two years in this example. This arithmetic excludes maintenance and other costs.

comparisons.title: A cheaper option can miss the need
comparisons.notice: The totals stay the same. The package now lacks a capability the shop requires.
comparisons.takeaway: A lower price does not supply a missing requirement. Capability, omitted costs and risks belong in the decision too.

scene: The interface says Saved, but the shop needs to know whether the intended visit actually changed.

comparisons.title: Inspect more than the toast
comparisons.notice: Keep the defect. Compare the message-only check with a check of both records.
comparisons.takeaway: The same defect can hide behind a passing toast check. A useful assertion inspects the intended change and the state that must stay unchanged.

comparisons.title: Correct the updater
comparisons.notice: Watch which record becomes confirmed. The other record should remain pending.
comparisons.takeaway: A relevant check should distinguish the faulty updater from the corrected one. A success message alone cannot do that.

scene: A customer submits a visit request. What should the browser say if it stops waiting before the response arrives?

comparisons.title: The response arrives too late
comparisons.notice: Compare the response delay with the client's waiting limit.
comparisons.takeaway: A timeout means the client stopped waiting. It does not establish whether the server stopped or whether a write happened.

comparisons.title: Give the client time to receive the response
comparisons.notice: Keep the server timing fixed and change only the waiting limit.
comparisons.takeaway: The response can now arrive within the model's waiting period. Real retries still need stable identity and evidence of the final state.

scene: Two customers are named Alex. After a restart, the shop also needs its records to remain available.

comparisons.title: A separate storage lifetime
comparisons.notice: Compare the retained records after the same process restart.
comparisons.takeaway: Process memory and persistent storage have different lifetimes. Persistence still needs its own protection, backup and recovery.

comparisons.title: One name, two identities
comparisons.notice: Compare two name matches with one exact identifier match.
comparisons.takeaway: A person's name may not uniquely select a record. A stable identifier can target the intended visit.

scene: Two booking operations compete for the last slot. Retries can also repeat a single intended operation.

comparisons.title: Protect the last slot
comparisons.notice: Inspect each operation's result. Accepted bookings must not exceed capacity.
comparisons.takeaway: A capacity check and reservation need a protected operation. Separate unprotected checks can both act on the same available slot.

comparisons.title: A retry is not a new intention
comparisons.notice: Keep four attempts. Change whether they share one operation identifier.
comparisons.takeaway: Stable retry identity lets repeated attempts refer to one intended operation instead of creating several reservations in this model.

scene: Customer C7 is signed in. That does not automatically allow access to C8's private visit.

comparisons.title: Signed in, different owner
comparisons.notice: The requesting identity stays signed in while the record owner changes.
comparisons.takeaway: Authentication identifies the caller. Authorization separately decides whether that caller may access this record.

comparisons.title: Remove the trusted check
comparisons.notice: Inspect whether a refused record becomes returned without permission.
comparisons.takeaway: A sign-in badge or hidden button cannot enforce the trusted record boundary. Removing the check can leak the fictional record.

scene: The shop wants to send a reminder through a provider. Configuration, acceptance and delivery are different facts.

comparisons.title: Configure before attempting
comparisons.notice: Compare zero provider attempts with an acknowledged attempt. No secret value is requested.
comparisons.takeaway: Required configuration permits an attempt in this model. Provider acceptance still does not establish delivery to a person.

comparisons.title: A timeout leaves uncertainty
comparisons.notice: Read the acceptance and delivery evidence separately after the response becomes ambiguous.
comparisons.takeaway: An ambiguous response is not a known failure or a verified delivery. A real system needs reconciliation rather than an invented success count.

scene: An executor is given a task, some authority and a budget. Each boundary has its own job.

comparisons.title: Enough budget to finish
comparisons.notice: Count the operations that run and the units that remain.
comparisons.takeaway: A permitted task can still stop at its budget. Increasing the budget makes this three-operation model task affordable.

comparisons.title: Money does not grant permission
comparisons.notice: Keep ample budget. Ask for an action outside the granted test authority.
comparisons.takeaway: The authority check refuses the action before spending budget. Extra resources do not expand permission.

scene: Two workstreams are building connected parts. They need a shared interface as well as time to coordinate.

comparisons.title: Agree on the field
comparisons.notice: Compare the key the interface expects with the key in the supplied payload.
comparisons.takeaway: Compatible field names let this local interface check fit. Speed elsewhere cannot repair a broken agreement between parts.

comparisons.title: More workers, one small task
comparisons.notice: Look for idle workers and additional coordination time.
comparisons.takeaway: One five-minute task still needs one work round. Extra workers add coordination in this model, so the total increases rather than decreases.

scene: An example response contains a neat date field, but the source never supplied a date.

comparisons.title: Keep an unknown fact unknown
comparisons.notice: The JSON can parse in both cases. Inspect the separate check for date support.
comparisons.takeaway: A valid shape does not establish a fact. Null can represent an unknown date without inventing certainty.

comparisons.title: Support must come from a source
comparisons.notice: Keep the response identical. Supply the matching date as fictional source evidence.
comparisons.takeaway: The source changes what the date check can support. This small rule still does not verify every claim in the summary or evaluate a real AI model.

scene: A helper retrieves a cancellation policy. A matching topic is only the beginning of checking whether it is usable.

comparisons.title: Relevant but too old
comparisons.notice: Keep the question fixed. Compare the document age with the allowed age.
comparisons.takeaway: Relevance and freshness answer different questions. This fictional policy now fits the model's age rule.

comparisons.title: An instruction inside a document
comparisons.notice: The source now asks to cancel the visit, but separate action authority is still absent.
comparisons.takeaway: Retrieved text supplies information. It cannot grant the user and policy authority required for an action.

scene: The helper flags urgent messages. The shop needs to inspect both false alerts and missed urgent cases.

comparisons.title: Raise the threshold
comparisons.notice: Inspect the same labelled cases before and after the threshold changes.
comparisons.takeaway: A threshold can reduce alerts while increasing missed positive cases. Precision and recall describe different parts of that tradeoff.

comparisons.title: Change the case mix
comparisons.notice: Keep the decision threshold. Add fictional positive cases to the evaluation sample.
comparisons.takeaway: The sample composition affects aggregate results. Record the labels, sample definition and mistakes that matter instead of quoting a metric without context.

scene: A regression check needs to notice a wrong-record update, including when the selected visit changes.

comparisons.title: Does the assertion see the defect?
comparisons.notice: Keep the updater faulty. Change the evidence the assertion inspects.
comparisons.takeaway: A passing weak check is not evidence that the relevant behaviour works. The record assertion exposes the deliberately faulty updater.

comparisons.title: Select the other record
comparisons.notice: The intended record changes. Does the assertion still identify the incorrect update?
comparisons.takeaway: A check should follow the selected record and protect the other one, rather than hard-coding one convenient identifier.

scene: A release changes code, configuration and possibly stored information. Those parts do not roll back together automatically.

comparisons.title: A release needs its configuration
comparisons.notice: The build passes in both cases. Inspect whether the required configuration is also present.
comparisons.takeaway: A passing build is one release condition. The running journey also needs its declared configuration and compatible data.

comparisons.title: Rollback only the code
comparisons.notice: Watch code change from v2 to v1 while the data schema remains v2.
comparisons.takeaway: Reverting code does not restore stored data. Under these declared rules, old code cannot read the migrated schema.

scene: A visit request feels slow. A trace helps you locate time before choosing what to change.

comparisons.title: Shorten one measured span
comparisons.notice: Keep database and validation time fixed. Watch the total and provider bar shrink.
comparisons.takeaway: A controlled change to one span changes this sequential total. A real incident still needs new observations to verify a proposed fix.

comparisons.title: Move the bottleneck
comparisons.notice: Look for the longest measured step after the database duration increases.
comparisons.takeaway: The relevant investigation can change with the evidence. A familiar explanation should not replace inspection of the current trace.

scene: The shop repeats the same read. Reuse can reduce source work, but the freshness rule affects what people receive.

comparisons.title: Refresh once, then reuse
comparisons.notice: The cached copy starts expired. Inspect the first source read and the later cache hits.
comparisons.takeaway: For these same-key, same-instant requests, the first read refreshes the copy and later reads reuse it. This is a model, not a service benchmark.

comparisons.title: Within its lifetime, already stale
comparisons.notice: The copy now passes the age rule even though the source changed after it was stored.
comparisons.takeaway: A cache lifetime is a reuse policy, not proof that a copy equals the current source. The model now returns stale cached answers.

scene: A change removed visit records. Having a snapshot, restoring it and checking the result are separate steps.

comparisons.title: Restore the snapshot
comparisons.notice: Compare the expected identifiers with the records after the chosen recovery.
comparisons.takeaway: A snapshot can supply the missing records in this local model. The restore label alone is still weaker than querying the recovered state.

comparisons.title: Check the recovered identifiers
comparisons.notice: The records stay present. Inspect the difference between an unrun check and completed identifier queries.
comparisons.takeaway: Recovery evidence includes whether the restored information is usable. Run the relevant checks instead of assuming a backup guarantees recovery.

scene: A maintenance team is preparing a site visit. The site needs approval before anyone can enter.

comparisons.title: Faster preparation, still blocked
comparisons.notice: Preparation gets faster. Watch whether the access gate opens.
comparisons.takeaway: Optimising a later step cannot satisfy a missing prerequisite. The approval requirement still blocks this model journey.

comparisons.title: Resolve the actual prerequisite
comparisons.notice: Keep preparation at one minute. Record the required approval and inspect the gate.
comparisons.takeaway: The journey can now proceed in the fictional scenario. A real investigation must establish who grants approval and how it is recorded.

scene: A public page is working. A new requirement asks it to share private customer records between users.

comparisons.title: Change the need
comparisons.notice: The static design stays the same while the required capability changes.
comparisons.takeaway: Files alone do not supply shared private records and trusted access control. The architecture needs suitable connected capabilities.

comparisons.title: Add a suitable connected design
comparisons.notice: Inspect the missing capability after the model design includes connected services.
comparisons.takeaway: The declared capabilities can now fit this simplified need. Actual security, implementation and operating responsibilities still need evidence.

scene: A dispatch tool saves one step, but creates correction work later. Only people who use it can experience either effect.

comparisons.title: Include the correction work
comparisons.notice: Keep the local saving and adoption fixed. Compare the whole workflow's net time.
comparisons.takeaway: Three scenario users now save 30 minutes and incur 9 correction minutes: 21 net minutes. These are assumptions, not measured benefits.

comparisons.title: What if nobody uses it?
comparisons.notice: The tool's stated per-person saving stays the same, but the active-person count changes.
comparisons.takeaway: With zero adoption, this model delivers zero net time saving. Investigate actual use before treating a feature's proposed saving as a result.

scene: A fresh operator will maintain the product, and a replacement provider uses a different field name.

comparisons.title: Make the replacement fit
comparisons.notice: Compare the expected key with the actual replacement payload and field assertion.
comparisons.takeaway: The local replacement check now fits its declared contract. A real operator still needs to demonstrate the actual journey and recovery.

comparisons.title: Compatible, but unchecked
comparisons.notice: Keep the field compatible. Remove the assertion run and inspect the evidence label.
comparisons.takeaway: A plausible contract is different from a performed check. An unrun assertion must remain unrun instead of inheriting a success claim.

scene: Your product faces a changed requirement. Trace what the new journey needs before adding components.

comparisons.title: A public page becomes a private journey
comparisons.notice: The existing components stay fixed. Inspect the capabilities the changed requirement now needs.
comparisons.takeaway: A previously adequate public-page design can miss a new private-record need. Identify the connected and permission boundaries instead of assuming the old path still fits.

comparisons.title: Give the helper a supporting source
comparisons.notice: The connected application is already present. Add the permitted supporting source and inspect the changed path.
comparisons.takeaway: A data store is not automatically supporting knowledge for an AI answer. This model fit still needs transfer to your own product and an independent review.
